title: What is end-to-end testing? Tools and best practices
summary: Learn what end-to-end testing is, how it compares to unit and integration testing, the top E2E tools, and how Greptile's TREX automates E2E tests on every PR.
body_markdown:
Many engineering teams today are over-reliant on unit tests and integration tests to catch bugs. Code is getting written at the speed of AI, but code review is lagging behind.


So teams cover their bases with a suite of integration tests, then hope for the best. But that leaves many bugs that you only discover end-to-end slipping through to prod.


Traditional end-to-end testing is slow, resource-intensive, and hard to maintain (not to mention, notoriously flaky), but AI is reshaping the ease, usage, and need for end-to-end testing. Here's what fast-moving engineering teams need to know.


## What is end-to-end (E2E) testing?


**End-to-end (E2E) testing validates the entire workflow from the user's perspective.** It tests your application in a real-world workflow. And it ensures that everything a user would need to complete an action (UI interactions, backend services, code, components, APIs, databases, etc.) is working together as expected.


End-to-end tests usually validate a specific workflow or feature, rather than a specific unit of code or component. For example, an E2E test might validate:


- If the user checkout flow works end-to-end, from adding an item to cart to the checkout confirmation page
- If the signup workflow works as expected
- If the user can effectively make changes to their profile


## End to end testing compared to other types of testing


E2E testing has traditionally been grouped with other types of automated testing in a model known as[the testing pyramid](https://www.greptile.com/content-library/testing-pyramid) .


**The testing pyramid is a model that helps software teams decide how to allocate resources to various types of testing.** At the base of the testing pyramid are unit tests, which are generally suggested to make up the bulk of your automated testing. In the middle are integration tests, and at the top, traditionally done sparingly, are E2E tests.


### End to end testing vs. unit testing


**End-to-end (E2E) testing validates the entire workflow from the user's perspective.** Unit tests test a small, individual function or component of the code.


- A unit test might ask "Does the submit button appear?" or "When *X* is clicked, does *Y* appear?"
- An E2E test might ask, "Does the user checkout flow work end-to-end?"


Both have a place in your automated test stack, but as your codebase grows in complexity and as teams integrate more agents and agentic coding workflows, you will need to simultaneously increase your proportion of E2E testing. It's easy to make a unit test pass, but making sure the code works with everything else it touches is a lot harder. E2E testing ensures that it does.


End to end testing Unit testing


Scope Tests an entire workflow end-to-end Tests a single unit of code in isolation


Output


Makes sure the user can take an expected action and all components work together properly


Makes sure the code works as expected or returns the expected output


Resources Traditionally more resource-intensive Very fast, easy to set up and maintain


Flakiness Typically more flaky Typically less flaky


Usage with AI Harder for agents to game Easy for agents to game and earn a "pass"


In short:


- **Use unit testing as you code as part of your automated testing within your CI/CD pipeline.** Use it to verify business logic, edge cases, error handling, and other small bugs that are related to specific code and components.
- **Use E2E testing before merging PRs or releasing new updates to validate user workflows.** Best for ensuring agent code integrates with your entire codebase, runtime validation, and catching complex bugs.


### End to end testing vs. integration testing


**End-to-end (E2E) testing validates the entire workflow from the user's perspective.** Integration testing tests a single connection between internal code or components and external services or APIs.


- An integration test might ask "Does our backend accurately connect to the payment processor API?" or "Does the authentication token service correctly parse and store user login data?"
- An E2E test might ask, "Does the user checkout flow work end-to-end?"


Both tests are useful: integration tests are faster and narrower in scope; E2E tests are more comprehensive.


End to end testing Integration testing


Scope Tests an entire workflow end-to-end


Tests a single connection between services, components, databases, etc.


Output


Makes sure the services communicate with each other properly


Resources Traditionally more resource-intensive Faster and optimized for local CI/CD pipelines


Usage with AI Harder for agents to game Easier for agents to game and earn a "pass"


Debugging More surface to find and catch bugs; debugging can be more complex


Narrower scope makes it easier to debug, but can miss more complex errors


In short:


- **Use integration testing when you need to ensure that specific services are working properly together.** Use it early in the development process, and favor it when you need fast, technical feedback as you build.
- **Use E2E testing when you need to ensure that new code works error-free across your entire codebase.** Favor it for agentic code and coding workflows, major features and user journeys, and before new releases.


## E2E testing benefits and drawbacks


Traditionally, the biggest drawbacks of E2E testing have been the time, resources, and maintenance needed to run them well. (This, of course, is changing with more automation and AI tools, like TREX, supporting E2E testing today.)


The benefits are only getting stronger, though. Here's a quick comparison:


Pros of E2E testing Cons of E2E testing


E2E testing


- Actually simulates the real user experience
- Validates complete business logic
-


Comprehensive testing of everything that goes into a workflow, feature, or action. Not just testing isolated code or components.


-


Catches bugs other types of testing miss. Complex bugs, cross-repo bugs, data-flow, security, or other logic failures often only show up at runtime.


- Reduces risk of high-impact failures post-deployment by running runtime validation before prod
-


Very difficult to "cheat" on because it tests the entire workflow, which makes it an excellent default for agentic code to ensure it works with your entire system


- Slower to run than unit or integration testing due to the number of pieces involved
- Spinning up sandbox or staging environments for E2E testing can be time-consuming or costly
- Debugging can be complex because there are so many elements being tested at once
-


Can be more prone to[test flakiness](https://www.greptile.com/content-library/flaky-tests) than other types of tests


## Is E2E testing worth it?


Suffice it to say that E2E testing has changed significantly in the last few years, as have our software development processes and coding workflows that determine what kinds of testing are needed in the first place.


In general, some level of E2E testing is always worth it (see again: the testing pyramid). Traditionally, a good rule of thumb was to have about 5-10% of your automated testing be end-to-end tests.


However, E2E testing is growing in popularity as more teams turn to[agentic coding](https://www.greptile.com/content-library/what-is-agentic-coding) as part of their development process. Agents are experts at writing dozens of unit tests that become flaky, or "cheating" on simpler tests that don't actually uncover bugs. E2E testing can verify that the code your agent wrote actually *works* for the end user when combined with all the other code that touches it in your codebase.


End-to-end testing is also generally more worth it when:


- **You're automating the E2E testing process.** This includes[spinning up sandboxes](https://www.greptile.com/content-library/what-is-a-sandbox) , writing and running the test, capturing artifacts, etc. Using a tool like TREX that automates this makes E2E far more efficient, effective, and usable for day-to-day work.
- **You're working with high complexity.** Complex workflows, codebases, or connections mean more surfaces for bugs to hide, and standard testing often doesn't catch these kinds of complex, cross-codebase bugs. E2E testing is more comprehensive and gives you far better validation.
- **You're looking for runtime validation.** E2E testing is one of the only testing types that can verify that things will work when you push them to prod, and there are plenty of bugs that only show up at runtime. The more bugs you see slipping through to prod, the more useful E2E is going to be for your team.
- **You're expanding agentic coding across your team.** E2E testing validates agentic code across a codebase no one knows end-to-end. When your team isn't writing the code, E2E testing becomes more valuable to verify that complex features work.


## How does end to end test automation work?


End-to-end testing spins up a test environment that models a real-world scenario, runs a real-world workflow from start to finish, and interacts with the application in the way a user would to validate that the entire application works together properly.


Here's how it works:


1. A sandboxing or test environment is deployed to set up the application stack. The frontend, backend, databases, and APIs are launched in a closed environment, either with production code or mocks/stubs.
2. A tester (manual) or agent (automated) clicks through the workflow in the test environment as a real user would: clicking buttons, filling out forms, submitting data, interacting with the application.
3. The system responds in the test environment as it would in a live production environment. Data is transferred, the system calls external APIs, databases are updated, the system returns a result, and so on.
4. The test checks if the expected results are returned. For example, if a tester adds an item to cart and checks out, is the inventory database updated appropriately, does the confirmation email trigger, etc.


With a great E2E automated testing setup, your agent or tool should also record, capture, and deliver artifacts that show what was tested, what happened, and where things went wrong (if they did).


For example,[TREX](https://www.greptile.com/trex) doesn't just tell you "ran checkout flow, found failure at checkout" or "signup flow worked as expected." Instead, it gives you a multi-artifact set for every TREX finding: screenshots, logs, API traces, execution scripts. This gives you a comprehensive picture of everything that was tested and what was found.


This gives you at least two major benefits:


1. **It makes debugging easy.** If the test failed, why? "Found failure at checkout" isn't helpful, and creates more manual review and debugging. An artifact that shows screenshots of the checkout process and API traces that log the exact place the flow went wrong helps you get to the heart of the issue, and fix it, quickly.
2. **It makes agents more trustworthy.** Agents are likely to hallucinate how thoroughly they've tested something, or to claim they got a certain result when they didn't. Artifacts help you verify every result the agent finds without re-running the tests.


## Best practices for E2E testing


-


**Make end-to-end tests clear, unique, and focused.** One test = one goal. And don't use an E2E test for something that could be tested adequately with a smaller test. As[Google's testing blog](https://testing.googleblog.com/2016/09/testing-on-toilet-what-makes-good-end.html) puts it:


> In order to be cost effective, an end-to-end test should focus on aspects of your system that cannot be reliably evaluated with smaller tests, such as resource allocation, concurrency issues and API compatibility.


This is still true in an agentic era, but keep in mind that AI code is often an aspect of your system that needs E2E testing more often (more on that later).


-


**Do E2E testing as soon as possible.** Don't put off E2E testing until the day before release when code is more or less finalized.[Shift testing left](https://www.greptile.com/content-library/shift-left-testing) and do E2E early, during the pull request stage, when bugs are cheaper and easier to fix.


-


**Use sandboxes, and mirror production environments.**[Sandboxing](https://www.greptile.com/content-library/what-is-a-sandbox) is a great solution for E2E testing, allowing you to run code in an isolated, controlled environment that can be spun up and then destroyed after the test. This keeps your tests clean and controlled (reducing test flakiness, which is more common on E2E tests), and allows you to mirror production environments exactly without risking real codebases on untested code.


-


**Make debugging easy by tracing artifacts.** Automated tests are only as strong as their verification. It's easy for AI tools to run a test and then say something like "checkout failed," but that tells you nothing about what went wrong or how to fix it. This has traditionally made debugging E2E tests time-consuming and tedious.[TREX](https://www.greptile.com/trex) runs and executes tests while tracing artifacts (screenshots, logs, scripts, videos, etc.) so you can see exactly what happened, what changed, and where things go wrong.


-


**Focus on real user goals and behaviors.** Don't test just to test. Focus on testing real user goals and behaviors from the user perspective.[Greptile's Computer Use](https://x.com/greptile/status/2115475319541150120) is one good way to do this. With Computer Use, TREX can run your application in desktop apps, web browsers, or a terminal. It can log in, click around as a user, use workflows, and more. This helps you focus on what users will actually care about and do, rather than just running a happy path flow.


## End to end testing tools


From traditional testing tools to more modern tools that use AI agents to speed up end-to-end testing, choosing the right E2E tool can make a big difference in how much E2E testing you're realistically able to do. Here's a quick breakdown of the top end-to-end testing tools:


**Playwright** is an open-source E2E web testing tool created by Microsoft. It works with TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, .NET, and Java. Each test runs in a clean, isolated browser context and automatically waits for interactive elements to load before proceeding, both features that help reduce E2E test flakiness.


Playwright's testing is fast and deterministic: you write a script, it runs it and gives you a pass/fail. It's good for verifying crucial business flows across browsers.


**Cypress** is an E2E testing tool that runs tests (written in JavaScript / TypeScript) inside the browser alongside your application code. It features automatic waiting, time-travel debugging, and element highlighting.


**Selenium** is a legacy E2E testing tool that is best for teams who need testing on older browsers or want to run a legacy testing suite. It doesn't feature automatic waiting and relies on third-party libraries for test runners, assertions, and parallel execution. However, it supports a wide range of languages and web browsers.


**Greptile** is a modern, autonomous AI code review and testing agent that[executes end-to-end testing via TREX](https://www.greptile.com/trex) . TREX looks at your PR, your repo and codebase context, test suite, and stack to figure out what needs to be tested, then spins up the sandbox with the appropriate tests, services, dependencies, and more to run your test end-to-end.


It can also use Computer Use to open a CLI or desktop terminal or web browser to run your application, click through it like a user would, and validate your code, start to finish. Along the way, it captures screenshots, logs, scripts, and other artifacts so you can see exactly what happened without re-running the test.

## How AI is changing E2E testing


AI and agentic coding are quickly shifting the *ease, methods,* and *need for* end-to-end testing.


You probably know that AI can make E2E testing easier with some new methods or tools (that's why you're reading this). But the need for end-to-end testing is also growing as agentic coding workflows do.


That's because agentic code is **riskier** than human-written code.[Not because it's worse](https://www.greptile.com/blog/rise-of-the-overnight-agents) , but because it often creates errors that humans don't, and thus don't know to look for. That makes AI-generated code harder to review ([even for the AI agent](https://www.greptile.com/blog/model-inversion) ).


Plus, the volume and velocity of code means human reviewers often can't keep up. And when new code is added to a codebase that, increasingly, no one knows end to end, it becomes easier to create unstable, brittle code that breaks once it touches other parts of your codebase.


That's why data from open-source, production repos looks like this:


- He et al.'s study of Cursor adoption in 806 GitHub repos found that velocity gains fade within two months of adoption. Meanwhile, **code complexity rises 41% at adoption and remains elevated** for the full observation period \[1\].
- Worse, Liu et al. tracked AI-introduced correctness and security issues across over 6,000 real production repositories from early 2025 through February 2026. Overall, out of 464,900 tracked AI-introduced issues, **22.7% still survived in the codebase in February 2026** \[2\].


Codebases are becoming more brittle, complex, and unsecured because many types of testing and review (linters, static analysis, unit tests, even integration testing) are easy for AI agents to "game." Agents will write code that passes lint and fails to compile. They write code that looks great on the surface, then breaks an old dependency in another repo. They write an easy unit test that passes, but forget about edge cases.


End-to-end testing is a great solution to all of this. You can't game it, because it forces you to validate that the code actually functions at runtime.


The more agentic coding you're doing, the more crucial it is to be doing E2E testing regularly. Not just on the top 10% most important workflows, but ideally, on anything coded agentically.


And how is *that* possible? With AI tools that make E2E easier, faster, and more efficient. We talked about some E2E testing tools above, and many of the legacy tools are still useful. But most teams *also* need AI-assisted E2E testing to match the velocity of agentic coding.

The goal with testing isn't simply *more* testing, but better testing. With TREX, we're making E2E testing more reliable, faster, and easier to do at scale, so that review stops being the backlog.
